Wastewater and Biosolids Treatment The City of Watsonville owns and operates a wastewater collection, treatment, and disposal system which provides sewerage service for a population of approximately 55,000 in an area that includes the City of Watsonville, the Santa Cruz County Freedom Sanitation District, the Santa Cruz County Salsipuedes Sanitary District, and the Monterey County Pajaro Sanitation District. The collection system encompasses 21 square miles and includes more than 170 miles of sanitary sewer lines which currently receive wastes discharged from residential, commercial, and 10 significant industrial facilities, including several food processors. Each member agency owns, operates, and maintains a sanitary sewer system that conveys wastewater to the Discharger’s force main for transport to the facility. Average daily influent flow ranges from 6.5 – 8.5 MGD. Treatment facilities consist of screening, pre-aeration/grit removal, primary sedimentation, biological filtration (trickling filters), odor control, solids contact stabilization (activated sludge), and secondary clarification. chunks.text: Wastewater is typically collected through sewage pipes in municipal areas. Treatment of wastewater entails a step-wise process that occurs in primary, secondary, and tertiary stages. Primary treatment involves basic screening and filtration processes to remove suspended solid waste and reduce its biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), which is an indicator to monitor water quality that assesses the amount of oxygen microorganisms must consume to break down the organic material present in wastewater (US EPA, 2012) . Primary treatment can reduce BOD by up to 30% (Flo ¨rke, 2013) . Secondary treatment uses biological processes to break down the dissolved organic matter remaining after primary treatment. Secondary treatment can remove up to 90% of BOD and total suspended solids (US EPA, 2004) . Any additional step in wastewater treatment is considered tertiary treatment (or ''advanced treatment''), which includes any purification process that continues beyond the previous steps and may require more complex technology such as ion exchange and reverse osmosis to further remove contaminants or phosphorous and nitrogen (World Bank, 2013b; US EPA, 2004) .

chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: Screens and grit removal are widely employed in WWTPs as they enhance the operation and maintenance of subsequent treatment units. Recent innovations in pretreatment technologies have brought the heavy cost of grit in WWTPs operations lower which has been considered an unavoidable burden. For example, based on advanced Grit Management™, Headcell® grit separation system was developed to achieve optimum grit removal for more than 30 years in the UK and USA. Headcell® is capable of achieving 95% removal of all grit 75 μm and larger. Because of its no-moving part design involving a hydraulically driven system, it delivers grit removal over a wide range of flows in a much smaller energy footprint than the conventional removal systems (Barter and Sherony, 2011) . chunks.text: A pilot plant comprised of primary (DAF) and secondary treatment unit (two stage trickling filters) was set up by Li et al. (1984) . Each trickling filter was 2.4 m high and consisted of media (surface area-98 m 2 /m 3 ). Around 40-50% oil and grease removal were achieved from DAF system. In case of trickling filters organic matter removal efficiencies were 70-85%. Apart from that, nitrification also resulted, but the process was entirely dependent upon loading rates. Intensive studies by Banks and Wang (2004) have shown that loading rates plays a vital role in biological treatment. Intensive studies conducted by them have shown that the organic matter removal efficiencies were 60-85% when operated at OLRs of 1.2-8.1 kg BOD/ m 3 -d for nine trickling filters.

chunks.text: Anaerobic digestion is a biological decomposition process used to treat, stabilise, and reduce the quantities of organic wastes prior to disposal or beneficial re-use. Anaerobic digestion has been used extensively in municipal wastewater treatment to stabilise primary sludge and activated sludge. Over the past decade, municipal wastewater treatment processes have adapted to meet reduced discharge limits on the effluent nitrogen concentration. Process adaptations include the removal of primary settlings and primary sludge streams; and increased retention times for biological nutrient removal (BNR) processes, resulting in increased sludge age. Increased sludge age results in waste activated sludge with inherently low degradability, as inert materials in the influent, as well inert decay products accumulate in the activated sludge (Gossett and Belser, 1982) . Adaptations of modern wastewater treatment processes have introduced new challenges for anaerobic digestion, as poor degradability of activated sludge requires long digester retention times, higher mixing costs, and also results in poor gas production. Incorporating a pre-treatment into anaerobic treatment may enhance the sludge digestion by accelerating hydrolysis, which is generally accepted as the rate-limiting step in anaerobic digestion.

chunks.text: There are already many types of mechanical dewatering processes, including press and vacuum filtration, centrifugation, etc. (Colin and Gazbar, 1995) . Mechanical dewatering energy consumption depends mainly on the structure of sludge flocs and the complex shear force between sludge and water, as well as different types of dewatering equipment and chemicals dosage, and is not dependent on the different origins of sludge (Novak, 2006) . The energy consumption of different processes varies from 15 to 179 kW,h/t DS (Wakeman, 2007) . The belt press filter, which has an energy consumption of about 60 kW,h/t DS (the moisture content of sludge is reduced from 99% to 80%), is extensively applied in China (Wakeman, 2007) .

chunks.text: The drying facility is located in a large Polish wastewater treatment plant and is composed of 4 lines. The scheme of one drying line is presented in Fig. 1 . Dewatered sludge is collected in a silo from where it is dosed to drum dryers. The temperature in the drum dryers is maintained at ca. 240-260 • C using hot oil. Sludge is uniformly distributed in the drum with paddles. The sludge retention time in the drier is 1-2 min, and the sludge layer in the drum is 1-2 cm thick. Water from the sludge is evaporated and flows as condensate with process air through a purification system composed of a Venturi orifice and two scrubbers, where it is then rinsed with the process water (secondary effluent from the wastewater treatment plant). The WWTP's treatment train is based on conventional activated sludge with nutrient removal, and 30% of the secondary effluent undergoes tertiary treatment for agricultural reuse (NPR-7) and to create a seawater intrusion barrier (after additional treatment processes).

chunks.text: In the activated sludge process the majority of biological solids removed in the secondary sedimentation tank are recycled (returned sludge). The feedback of most of the cell yields from the sedimentation tank encourages rapid adsorption of the pollutants in the incoming settled sewage and also serves to stabilize the operation over a wide range of dilution rates and substrate concentrations imposed by fluctuations in the flow and strength of the wastewater. Secondary treatment processes can remove up to 95 per cent of the BOD and suspended solids entering the process, as well as significant amounts of heavy metals and certain organic compounds which could otherwise cause the deterioration of chemical and ecological quality of receiving waters [10, 53] . Conventional wastewater treatment usually ends with secondary treatment which cannot efficiently remove all the different compounds found in sewage and therefore treated effluents are one of the main sources of persistent micropollutants in the environment [1, 62] . For water reuse, tertiary treatment is needed to provide additional removal of contaminants such as microbial pathogens, particulates, or nutrients, and advanced treatment processes are employed when wastewater is to be reclaimed for reuse, depending on the type of use and quality requirements [49] .

chunks.text: Based on a survey on pre-treatment measures for 17 full-scale AeMBRs, the following information deserves special attention (Itokawa et al., 2008) : 1) grit chamber, coarse and fine screenings are mostly essential for MBR operation to removal grits, large suspended particles and long fibers, with fine screening (3 mm for FS membrane and 0.5-1 mm for HF membrane) installed universally; and 2) using the "by pass sieving" method, which recycles part of the suspended sludge through a sieve, achieves the further removal of unfavorable substances accumulated in the bioreactor. These means can be extended to AnMBRs minimizing the presence of undesirable substances into the bioreactor while with adequate consideration of keeping strict anaerobic environment. A recent novel concept, referred to as wastewater pre-concentration (Ansari et al., 2016) , is still under investigation, but has shown great potential to enhance bioresource recovery and energy generation efficiency (Guven et al., 2019) , accompanied by a low volumetric flow rate and process footprint (Alvarado et al., 2020) .
